issues.legal_issue: The organised-crime requirements do not demand that every prior charge-sheeted activity have a pecuniary objective, and an objective of gaining supremacy or another undue advantage may qualify.
material_facts: The appellant was named in several prior charge-sheeted cases involving violence or other unlawful conduct, some with the alleged syndicate leader and recurring co-accused.
The alleged activities included offences against persons and property, rioting with weapons, intimidation and offences under arms legislation.

The current complaint alleged kidnapping, threats and demands for money and property, while the prior activities were also said to have been aimed at establishing supremacy and gaining other advantages.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that each prior case had to allege a pecuniary objective. Actual violence is not indispensable where the activity involves a threat of violence, intimidation, coercion or other unlawful means, and an advantage may include establishing supremacy rather than a direct financial gain.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(1)(d), 2(1)(e) and 2(1)(f) of the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999, the requirements are assessed together: continuing unlawful activity involves qualifying cognizable offences, charge-sheets and cognizance; organised crime involves the specified unlawful means and an objective of pecuniary benefit or undue economic or other advantage; and an organised crime syndicate is a group of two or more persons engaging in organised crime. The Court endorsed State of Maharashtra v. Jagan Gagansingh Nepali @ Jagya (2011) SCC OnLine Bom 1049, which held that “other advantage” is not confined by ejusdem generis to pecuniary or economic gain, and applied Ranjitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma v. State of Maharashtra (2005) 5 SCC 294. Strict construction, as discussed in State of Maharashtra v. Lalit Somdatta Nagpal (2007) 4 SCC 171 and Balram Kumawat v. Union of India (2003) 7 SCC 628, does not justify an interpretation that defeats the law’s purpose.

rule.if: special_crime_law_review and continuing_activity_threshold and group_linked_activities and organised_means and pecuniary_or_other_undue_advantage_objective

predicates.special_crime_law_review: The court is reviewing whether a special organised-crime law applies to alleged criminal activity.
predicates.continuing_activity_threshold: More than one qualifying cognizable offence by the relevant person or group has been charge-sheeted and cognizance has been taken.
predicates.group_linked_activities: The alleged activities link recurring participants as members of a group or as acting on its behalf.
predicates.organised_means: The alleged activity involves violence, a threat of violence, intimidation, coercion or another unlawful means.
predicates.pecuniary_or_other_undue_advantage_objec: The alleged activity has an objective of financial gain or another undue economic or other advantage, such as establishing supremacy.

issues.definition: When a special organised-crime review concerns qualifying repeated activity linked to a group, carried out by specified unlawful means for financial or other undue advantage, the organised-crime requirements are satisfied even if every prior activity was not aimed at pecuniary gain.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal or quashing of a prior case does not by itself prevent the charge-sheeted activity from counting toward the continuing-unlawful-activity requirement.
material_facts: Charge-sheets had been filed and cognizance taken in prior cases involving the appellant and other recurring alleged group members.
One prior case ended in acquittal after a witness turned hostile and other witnesses, including the complainant and injured person, did not appear.
Another prior case was quashed after the parties settled a cross-case dispute.
issues.conclusion: The outcomes of acquittal and quashing did not disqualify those cases for the continuing-unlawful-activity assessment; the relevant considerations were the qualifying activity, filing of charge-sheets and taking of cognizance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(1)(d) of the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999 focuses on qualifying cognizable activity, charge-sheets filed before a competent court and cognizance taken. The result of an individual case is not decisive for that assessment. The Court also noted the witness-protection purpose reflected in Section 19 when discussing the acquittal resulting from witnesses not supporting or appearing for the prosecution.

predicates.special_crime_law_review: The court is reviewing whether prior activity meets the continuing-activity threshold for a special organised-crime prosecution.
predicates.qualifying_chargesheet_and_cognizance: A qualifying cognizable offence was charge-sheeted before a competent court and cognizance was taken.
predicates.prior_case_ended_without_conviction: The prior case ended in acquittal, discharge or quashing rather than a conviction.

issues.definition: In a review of continuing criminal activity, a qualifying charge-sheeted offence remains relevant to the threshold even when the prior case ended without a conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A prosecution sanction is not invalid for want of application of mind when the order, read as a whole, demonstrates consideration of relevant material and satisfaction of the statutory requirements.
material_facts: The sanction order recounted the appellant’s prior cases, recurring co-accused, alleged syndicate links and evidence collected in the current investigation.
The authority recorded satisfaction that the accused were members of an organised crime syndicate and had committed qualifying activity for pecuniary or other advantage.
The appellant argued that the authority had merely repeated statutory expressions and had not separately recorded satisfaction about the syndicate.
issues.conclusion: The Court found the sanction order meticulous and sufficient when read in its entirety, and held that the authority had applied its mind to the relevant material and requirements.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(2) of the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999 requires prior sanction by an appropriately ranked police officer before a Special Court takes cognizance. The Court applied the combined requirements of Sections 2(1)(d), (e) and (f), and the principles in Lalit Somdatta Nagpal and Kavitha Lankesh v. State of Karnataka (2021) SCC OnLine SC 956: the authority must assess whether the material reveals organised crime by a syndicate; the order is considered in its entirety, and strict adherence does not turn on isolated wording. Jagannath Misra v. State of Orissa (1966) 3 SCR 134 was distinguished because the present order showed careful consideration rather than casual or mechanical satisfaction.

rule.if: prosecution_sanction_review and authority_considered_relevant_material and authority_recorded_reasoned_satisfaction and order_shows_application_of_mind_as_a_whole

predicates.prosecution_sanction_review: The court is reviewing a prior sanction for prosecution under a special organised-crime law.
predicates.authority_considered_relevant_material: The sanctioning authority considered the relevant case history and evidence placed before it.
predicates.authority_recorded_reasoned_satisfaction: The authority recorded satisfaction on the essential features of the alleged organised criminal activity and syndicate.
predicates.order_shows_application_of_mind_as_a_who: The order, read as a whole rather than by isolating a phrase, reflects consideration of the matter.

issues.definition: A prosecution sanction is not invalid for non-application of mind when the authority considers relevant material, records satisfaction on the essential features, and the order as a whole reflects that consideration.

issues.legal_issue: A sanctioning authority may consider co-accused confessional statements that implicate the accused when forming its view, particularly where those statements are not the sole basis for sanction.
material_facts: Two co-accused, including the alleged syndicate leader, made confessional statements describing the alleged offences and the appellant’s role.
The sanction order also referred to other evidence collected in the investigation, including witness statements and physical or electronic material.
The appellant was jointly accused with the persons who made the statements.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no error in the sanctioning authority’s consideration of the confessional statements as part of the evidence, given the appellant’s status as a co-accused and the other material considered.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18 of the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999 overrides Sections 25 and 26 of the Evidence Act, 1872 for confessions within its scope, but their use is limited to the confessor and a co-accused, abettor or conspirator. Relying on State of Maharashtra v. Kamal Ahmed Mohammed Vakil Ansari (2013) 12 SCC 17, the Court held that the statements’ relevance to the appellant was not wholly irrelevant because he was a co-accused; they formed part, rather than the entirety, of the material considered at sanction.

rule.if: prosecution_sanction_review and coaccused_confession_implicates_person and authority_considered_other_evidence and confession_was_not_the_sole_basis

predicates.prosecution_sanction_review: The court is reviewing a sanction decision made before prosecution under a special organised-crime law.
predicates.coaccused_confession_implicates_person: A person jointly accused in the case made a confession that implicates the person whose prosecution is being considered.
predicates.authority_considered_other_evidence: The authority also considered evidence apart from the confession.
predicates.confession_was_not_the_sole_basis: The authority did not rely exclusively on the confession in reaching its view.

issues.definition: A co-accused’s confession may support a sanction assessment when it implicates the person concerned and the authority also considers other evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A person declared an absconder who remains beyond the investigating agency’s reach ordinarily does not merit indulgence under the Supreme Court’s extraordinary appellate jurisdiction.
material_facts: A proclamation had been issued declaring the appellant an absconder after he remained out of reach of the investigating agency.
The appellant sought relief from the Supreme Court while disputing the prosecution sanction.
The Court considered the appeal on its merits but also stated that the appellant’s absconder status ordinarily warranted no indulgence.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that a declared absconder who remains out of reach ordinarily deserves no concession or indulgence, and that the challenge ought to fail; it nevertheless examined and rejected the appeal on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a person who remains out of reach and stands in conflict with the legal process ordinarily should not receive discretionary relief under Article 136 of the Constitution of India. It stated that the principle applied to pre-arrest bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, including Prem Shankar Prasad v. State of Bihar (2021) SCC OnLine SC 955, applies with greater force to Article 136 relief.

predicates.supreme_court_extraordinary_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking discretionary relief from the Supreme Court.
predicates.applicant_declared_absconder: A court or competent authority has formally declared the applicant an absconder.
predicates.applicant_remains_out_of_reach: The applicant remains beyond the reach of the investigating agency and has not submitted to the process of law.

issues.definition: In an extraordinary Supreme Court appeal, a declared absconder who remains out of reach ordinarily does not receive discretionary relief.
